intent: Make the relationship between every pair of bounded contexts explicit — who is upstream, who translates, who conforms, who deliberately does not integrate — before the dependencies become expensive to change.
problem: Integrations between contexts grow organically, each with its own implicit semantics; nobody knows who owns the contract, who may change it, or whether a model is being translated or adopted wholesale, so a change in one context breaks another in a way nobody predicted.
context: The context map is the strategic-design artifact that shows how bounded contexts relate, both organisationally and integration-wise. Evans groups the patterns into cooperation (partnership, shared kernel), customer-supplier (conformist, anti-corruption layer, open host service) and separate ways (duplicate functionality). A context map usually names both the integration pattern (technical shape) and the organisational relationship (political), and the useful questions are: who drives changes, can we translate the upstream model or do we conform, is the upstream's interface stable enough for many consumers, and are both contexts equally coupled. A map that is drawn once and never revisited is worse than none, because it asserts something false.
benefits: Every cross-context dependency has a named owner and a named relationship.
The cost of an integration becomes visible before it is paid, not after.
The team relationship (who negotiates) is separated from the technical shape (who translates).
Gaps in the model — an integration nobody can justify, an upstream with five ad-hoc consumers — become visible as such.
Onboarding a new context means reading the map, not reverse-engineering the code.
tradeoffs: The map is a model of an organisation and goes stale as quickly as the organisation changes.
Choosing a relationship is a political decision as much as a technical one, and the map records the decision without resolving it.
Drawing a thorough map is real work, and for a small system it is not worth the effort.
A map can legitimise a bad integration by giving it a name.
Maps drawn as one-off design documents rather than living artifacts decay immediately.
quality_attributes_note: type_safety 4 — a context map is documentation and an organisational artifact, not a checked constraint. discoverability 9 because it is the map new engineers read first.

participants.responsibility: A node on the map; owns one model.
participants.notes: Each node is typically labelled with its subdomain classification (core / supporting / generic).

participants.responsibility: The typed edge: partnership, shared kernel, customer-supplier, conformist, ACL, OHS+PL, or separate ways.
participants.notes: An edge should name both the organisational relationship and the technical shape.

participants.responsibility: The context others depend on; its changes propagate.
participants.notes: Upstream/downstream is the asymmetry that makes customer-supplier and conformist distinct.

participants.responsibility: The consumer; decides whether to translate or conform.
participants.notes: Multiple downstream consumers of one upstream is what an open host service consolidates.

use_cases: Recording that Sales conforms to the canonical Customer model in a legacy system.
Discovering that one upstream context has five bespoke integrations and needs an open host service.
Deciding that an integration nobody can justify should become separate ways.
Exposing that a supposed partnership is actually one team dictating to another.
Marking a legacy area as a big ball of mud so its boundary is contained rather than untangled.
avoid_when: The system is a single context with no integrations — there is no map to draw.
It would be a one-off artifact rather than something the team maintains.
The exercise is being used to legitimise a predetermined service split.
pitfalls: Drawing the map after the fact and calling it the design; by then it records accidents.
Naming the technical pattern without naming the organisational relationship, which is where the cost lives.
Leaving the big ball of mud off the map because it is embarrassing.
Treating each edge independently — an upstream with five customers is a design problem the edges hide.
Never revisiting the map when a team or a system changes.

related_patterns_notes.bounded-context: The nodes of the context map are bounded contexts.
related_patterns_notes.conformist: One of the typed edges on the map: downstream adopts the upstream model wholesale.
related_patterns_notes.customer-supplier: One of the typed edges: downstream has negotiating power but the supplier decides.
related_patterns_notes.separate-ways: One of the typed edges, and the deliberate choice to have none.
related_patterns_notes.shared-kernel: One of the typed edges, sitting between partnership and separate ways in cost.

anti_patterns: A context map with no edges that matches no reality.
Unnamed edges ("they call each other somehow").
Using Conformist when an anti-corruption layer is warranted, importing the upstream model wholesale.
Using a shared kernel for shared utility code, which is not a shared domain model.
Mapping the technical integration while leaving the team relationship implicit.
design_principles: DDD groups the integration patterns by the nature of team collaboration: cooperation, customer-supplier, and separate ways.
Context Mapping identifies and defines the boundaries of different domains within a larger system and visualises how they interact.
A context map usually names both the integration pattern (technical) and the organisational relationship (political).
Test at the context boundaries; organize and document context maps as living artifacts.
Shared kernel is appropriate only when duplication cost exceeds coordination cost.
best_practices: Label every edge with both the pattern and the organisational reality.
Ask the four questions before naming an edge: who drives changes, can we translate or must we conform, is the interface stable for many consumers, are both sides equally coupled.
Keep the map in the repository next to the code and revisit it whenever a context is added.
Mark big ball of mud explicitly so it is contained rather than quietly expanded.
Prefer an anti-corruption layer to conformism whenever the downstream model matters.
